writtenQuestions.text: Q9.1. What are the main branches of Physics? State briefly.
modelAnswer: Mechanics: It is a study of motion and the physical effects which influence motion.

Acoustics: It deals with the nature and physical aspects of audible sound energy.
Optics: It deal with the physical aspects of visible light.
Electromagnetism: It is the study of electromagnetic phenomenon and mutual relationship between electric current and magnetic field.
Quantum Mechanics: It explains the behaviour of particles at the atomic and subatomic level.

Relativistic Mechanics: It explains how space and time are not absolute quantities but related to observer. It describes the relationship between them and how they are influenced by gravity and speed.
Nuclear Physics: It is the study of the properties of nuclei of the atoms.
Particle Physics: It is the study of subatomic particles and elementary particles which are basic building blocks of matter.
Astronomy: It is study of distribution of celestial bodies like planets, stars and galaxies.
Cosmology: It explores the large structure and evolution of the universe.
Solid State Physics: It is the study of some specific properties of matter in solid form.

explain.title: Observation and hypothesis
explain.body: The first step is to observe a natural process and collect data. From those observations, suggest an explanation that can be tested: this is a hypothesis. For example, observing a shadow can lead to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.

explain.title: Experiment
explain.body: “Experiment is an organized repeatable process which is used to test the truth of a hypothesis.” In the cardboard example, aligned holes let torchlight pass, while a displaced hole blocks it.

explain.title: Theory and prediction
explain.body: After an assumption is successfully verified by careful experimentation, it becomes a theory that applies to similar phenomena. Careful analysis of a theory can then be used to predict unknown aspects of nature. If test results do not agree with a prediction, the hypothesis is changed or rejected.

explain.title: Falsifiability
explain.body: A scientific theory must make predictions that can be tested and potentially proven false. This requirement prevents theories from relying on vague or untestable claims.

explain.title: Law
explain.body: “When a theory has been tested many times and generally accepted as true, it is called a law.” A law explains observations and experiments of the past and can predict other aspects of nature. Theories and laws may still be modified or disproved when science brings new facts and insights.

mistakes: Do not mix up an observation, which records what happens, with a hypothesis, which suggests an explanation.
Do not call a hypothesis a theory before it has been tested and successfully verified through careful experimentation.
Do not say that one successful test proves a prediction will always be correct; repeated tests over similar situations are important.
Do not describe a law as an unchangeable ultimate truth; the section says scientific theories and laws can be modified or disproved.
Do not confuse falsifiability with proving a theory false: it means the theory can be tested and could potentially be proven false.

explain.title: Science and its groups
explain.body: Science is a way of studying the natural world by using investigation and evidence. Its two broad groups are physical science and life science. Physics belongs to physical science.

explain.title: Physics and its branches
explain.body: Physics studies matter, energy, and their interactions. Its branches include mechanics, heat, sound, light, and electricity and magnetism. These ideas support many technologies and engineering applications.

explain.title: Scientific method
explain.body: Scientists ask questions, propose hypotheses, make predictions, test ideas, collect and analyse data, and draw conclusions. Investigations may use observation, experimentation, or research.

explain.title: Theories, laws, and evidence
explain.body: A theory is an evidence-supported explanation; a law describes a regular pattern in nature. Neither should be treated as beyond examination: new evidence can lead scientists to revise ideas.

explain.title: Falsifiability and collaboration
explain.body: A scientific claim must be open to testing that could show it to be wrong. Complex questions may involve several fields, so researchers with different kinds of scientific knowledge collaborate.

mistakes: Do not describe a hypothesis as a proven fact; it is a possible answer that needs investigation.
Do not say that a theory is simply a guess; a scientific theory is supported by evidence.
Do not confuse a theory with a law: a theory explains, while a law describes a regular pattern.
Do not claim that one confirming result proves a prediction is always correct; further testing is needed.
Do not conclude that an untestable hypothesis is automatically false; it cannot be scientifically checked without a test.
When describing the scientific method, do not leave out testing, data analysis, or the conclusion.

notes.title: The scope of physics
notes.answer: Physics is a fundamental science about matter, energy, space, time, and their connections and interactions.
notes.explanation: Physics studies matter, energy, space, time, and how they are connected. It is a basic part of the physical sciences. Its branches study different parts of nature, and some combine physics with other subjects.
notes.simple: Physics helps us understand how things in the universe behave, from tiny particles to stars and galaxies.
examples: Classical mechanics studies motion and forces.
Astrophysics uses physics to study stars and other objects in space.
steps: Identify the topic being studied, such as motion, heat, light, or particles.

notes.title: Branches of Physics
notes.answer: Optics studies the physical aspects of visible light.
notes.explanation: Physics has different branches because each branch studies a particular kind of physical phenomenon. For example, optics studies visible light, while acoustics studies audible sound.
notes.simple: Physics is divided into branches. Each branch focuses on a different part of the physical world.
examples: A prism separating white light into colours is studied in optics.
The properties of an atom’s nucleus are studied in nuclear physics.

notes.title: Interdisciplinary Nature of Physics
notes.answer: Interdisciplinary physics is the integration and interaction of physics with other fields of study. Its fields include biophysics, medical physics, astrophysics, geophysics, climate physics and computation physics.
notes.explanation: Physics connects with other fields when its principles and methods are used to study questions in those fields. For example, medical physics uses physics for health diagnosis and treatment, while geophysics uses it to study Earth.
notes.simple: Interdisciplinary physics means using physics together with another subject to study or solve a problem.
examples: MRI is an example of medical physics.
Studying earthquakes using physical principles is an example of geophysics.
steps: Identify what is being studied: health, living things, space, Earth, climate, or a complex physical problem.
Match it to the relevant field: medical physics, biophysics, astrophysics, geophysics, climate physics, or computation physics.
Give a relevant example, such as MRI for medical physics or earthquakes for geophysics.

notes.title: Interdisciplinary Research
notes.answer: Interdisciplinary research combines knowledge and methods from different fields to address complex issues and foster innovation.
notes.explanation: Interdisciplinary research brings together knowledge and methods from different fields of science. This helps scientists solve complex problems, develop new ideas and share knowledge more quickly.
notes.simple: When a problem is too big for one subject, experts from different subjects work together.
examples: Understanding climate change uses knowledge from meteorology, oceanography, physics, chemistry, biology and environmental sciences.
Nanotechnology combines physics, chemistry, material science and engineering.
steps: Identify the complex issue or research goal.
Bring together the relevant fields of knowledge and expertise.
Share findings and methods, and work together on possible solutions.

notes.title: Scientific Method: From Observation to Law
notes.answer: The scientific method uses observations and experiments to test hypotheses, build theories, make predictions, and, after repeated testing, formulate laws.
notes.explanation: The scientific method is a sequence for investigating a problem: observe, suggest a hypothesis, test it, and use the results to develop explanations and predictions. Repeated successful testing may lead to a law, but scientific ideas can still be changed when new evidence appears.
notes.simple: Observe something, suggest an explanation, and test it. Use the evidence to improve the explanation and make predictions.
examples: Observing a shadow leads to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.
If the holes in a row of cardboards are aligned, torchlight passes through; if one cardboard is moved, the light is blocked.
steps: Identify or recognize an issue or a problem.
Gather information through observations of its various aspects.
Propose an explanation or a guess work known as hypothesis.
Perform experiment or collect evidences to test the hypothesis.
Record, organize and analyze gathered data, plotting and interpreting graphs to reach at a conclusion which is called a theory.
Repeated tests of the theory to wide range of similar issues then lead towards the formulation of a law.
notes.checkQuestion: What must be true of a scientific theory for it to be falsifiable?
notes.checkAnswer: A scientific theory must make predictions that can be tested and could potentially be shown to be false.

notes.title: Scientific knowledge in technology and engineering
notes.answer: Physics provides the scientific principles used in technology and engineering.
notes.explanation: Physics provides scientific principles used in technology and engineering. Technology uses scientific knowledge to develop methods and techniques. Engineering applies scientific principles and technologies to design and build things for specific needs, while also considering cost and safety.
notes.simple: Science helps us understand how things work. Technology uses that knowledge to make methods, machines or programmes. Engineering uses scientific knowledge and technology to design useful things.
examples: Automobile technology is based on the principles of thermodynamics.
A civil engineer designs bridges to withstand strong winds, earthquakes, intense weather conditions and heavy traffic.
steps: Identify the technology, such as automobile, radar or laser technology.

notes.title: Nature of Science
notes.answer: Science is the systematic study of the natural world using observation, investigation, and evidence.
notes.explanation: Science studies the natural world through observation, investigation, and evidence. Physics is a physical science concerned with matter, energy, and their interactions. Scientific ideas are tested: a hypothesis is a possible answer to a question, while a theory is a well-supported explanation and a law describes a regular pattern in nature. Scientific knowledge can change when new evidence requires a theory or law to be modified.
notes.simple: Science is a way of learning about nature by asking questions and checking ideas with evidence.
examples: Observing that a plant near a window grows towards the light is an observation.
A prediction might be: if the plant receives more light, it will grow faster.
steps: Ask a question about something you observe.
Suggest a possible answer (hypothesis).
Make a prediction from the hypothesis.
Test the prediction through investigation or an experiment.
Collect and analyse the data.
Use the evidence to support, reject, or modify the hypothesis.
notes.checkAnswer: A hypothesis is a possible answer to a question that can be tested.

written.text: Q9.1. What are the main branches of Physics? State briefly.
modelAnswer: Mechanics: It is a study of motion and the physical effects which influence motion.

Acoustics: It deals with the nature and physical aspects of audible sound energy.
Optics: It deal with the physical aspects of visible light.
Electromagnetism: It is the study of electromagnetic phenomenon and mutual relationship between electric current and magnetic field.
Quantum Mechanics: It explains the behaviour of particles at the atomic and subatomic level.

Particle Physics: It is the study of subatomic particles and elementary particles which are basic building blocks of matter.
Astronomy: It is study of distribution of celestial bodies like planets, stars and galaxies.
Cosmology: It explores the large structure and evolution of the universe.
Solid State Physics: It is the study of some specific properties of matter in solid form.

written.text: What is the relationship between an experiment and a hypothesis?
modelAnswer: A hypothesis is a proposed explanation or guess based on observations or experiments.
An experiment is an organized repeatable process.
It is used to test the truth of the hypothesis.
The results provide evidence that may lead the hypothesis to be accepted, changed or rejected.

written.text: What is scientific method? Describe its main steps with examples.
modelAnswer: Scientific method is a systematic approach used to search for truth of an issue and problem solving regarding natural and physical world.
First, identify a problem and gather information by observation.
Next, propose a hypothesis and perform an experiment or collect evidence to test it.
Record, organize and analyse the data to reach a conclusion called a theory; repeated tests of the theory over similar issues lead towards a law.
For example, observation of shadows leads to the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line.
When holes in four cardboards are aligned with a torch, light passes through; when one cardboard is displaced, the light is blocked.
This experiment supports the hypothesis that light travels in a straight line, and repeated testing in different situations may establish a law.
written.followUp: What is a hypothesis? Give an example.

rubric.why: A correct definition frames the entire process.
rubric.how: Describe it as a systematic approach to investigating problems in the natural and physical world.

rubric.description: Give the early steps in order.

rubric.why: Testing and analysing evidence are essential steps between hypothesis and theory.
rubric.how: Explain that the hypothesis is tested and the data analysed to reach a theory.

rubric.why: The section's example demonstrates how an experiment tests the hypothesis.

rubric.description: State how the process leads towards a law.
rubric.why: Repeated tests connect the example to the final stage of scientific method.
rubric.how: Mention repeated testing of the theory in similar situations.

written.text: Differentiate the terms, science, technology and engineering with examples.
modelAnswer: Science is a collective knowledge about the natural phenomena and events.
Technology refers to the methods and techniques developed by using scientific knowledge; for example, automobile technology is based on the principles of thermodynamics.
Engineering is the process of applying various technologies and scientific principles to design various instruments, tools and build things that help to meet specific needs.
For example, a civil engineer designs a bridge that can withstand strong winds, earthquakes, intense weather conditions and heavy traffic.

written.text: Q9.8. What is falsifiability concept? How is it important?
modelAnswer: Falsifiability means that a scientific idea can be tested in a way that could show it to be wrong.
It is important because a claim that cannot possibly be tested or disproved cannot be evaluated scientifically.

written.text: Q9.1. Is the theory of science an ultimate truth? Describe briefly.
modelAnswer: No, a scientific theory is not an ultimate truth.
It is a well-supported explanation based on available evidence.

written.text: Q9.4. Describe when a theory is rejected or needs its modification.
modelAnswer: A theory needs modification when new observations or experimental results do not agree with part of its explanation.
Scientists test the theory against further evidence.
If only part of the explanation conflicts with the evidence, that part may be modified.
If reliable evidence repeatedly contradicts its main claims, the theory may be rejected.
